title: Google DeepMind releases AlphaGenome 2 to predict DNA variant effects at single-cell resolution
subtitle: The successor to AlphaGenome moves from bulk-tissue predictions to specific cell types, reports recovering 30 percent of causal variants on the TenK10K immune dataset versus 16 percent for the prior approach, and ships via the AlphaGenome API for non-commercial research.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome 2 on November 11, pushing its DNA-variant prediction model from bulk-tissue outputs to cell-type and cell-state resolution. The model is trained on more than 100 million single-cell profiles across 68 tissues in humans and mice and conditions each prediction on a chosen tissue, cell type, or cell state, so researchers can ask how a specific variant will alter gene activity inside, say, a CD8 T cell rather than averaging across whole-blood samples. On the TenK10K single-cell eQTL benchmark, DeepMind reports recovering 30 percent of causal variants against 16 percent for the prior fine-tuned approach, and the model beats fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1, Borzoi, and Scooby on both single-cell eQTL and enhancer-gene benchmarks. Access is free for non-commercial research through the AlphaGenome API; weights are not released, and private previews are rolling out to commercial genomics and drug-discovery partners, with Genomics Limited announcing integration into its Mystra platform.

The move from bulk to single-cell matters because disease biology is cell-type specific. A variant that looks neutral when averaged across a tissue can be dominant in one cell lineage — a particular neuronal subtype, a specific immune cell, a cancer precursor — and bulk assays have historically missed those signals. AlphaGenome 2 also accepts new single-cell data from as few as a few dozen cells and will produce predictions for that cell state without retraining, which is the practical hinge for most labs: fine-tuning a genome model is an engineering project, feeding it a small local reference dataset is not. The architecture is the same underlying transformer approach as AlphaGenome 1 scaled with much richer conditioning, which is the pattern DeepMind has run across AlphaFold, AlphaMissense, and AlphaGenome — add a biologically meaningful conditioning signal, keep scaling.

This lands as the single-cell field is becoming the dominant frame in human genetics. The Human Cell Atlas crossed 100 million annotated cells earlier this year, and the Broad, Sanger, EMBL and Chan Zuckerberg Initiative have each shifted their flagship efforts toward cell-state resolution. Pharma pipelines for rare and immune diseases are being rebuilt around the same lens, and tools that connect genetic variants to cell-specific effects are the critical missing layer between GWAS hits and drug targets. AlphaGenome 2 is not approved for clinical or diagnostic use, and the paper's specifics on uncertainty quantification will matter more than the headline recovery numbers; expect the first independent replications and ablations to show up in bioRxiv within a month.

A takeaway for learners: genomics AI is a good example of where the next decade of applied machine learning lives. The models are smaller than frontier language models, the data is public, the benchmarks are improving fast, and the biology constrains the problem in ways that make evaluation honest. If you want a technical track that is less crowded than the chat-model race and has a clear scientific payoff, work through the AlphaGenome tutorials, read one of the eQTL papers end to end, and try to replicate a figure on a laptop. The tools are closer to open than the frontier LLM stack, and the field is still short on people who can speak both ML and molecular biology fluently.
